titleText.es: Es decir, ¿qué es más probable, que hayas descubierto errores fundamentales en esta disciplina que nadie había pensado antes, o que necesites leer un poco más? Pista: es lo que requiere menos trabajo.
titleText.en: I mean, what's more likely -- that I have uncovered fundamental flaws in this field that no one in it has ever thought about, or that I need to read a little more?  Hint: it's the one that involves less work.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive; the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute, including its original spacing.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, LA CIENCIA ES UN PROCESO ABIERTO EN EL QUE CUALQUIERA PUEDE APORTAR BUENAS IDEAS.

applications.explanationEn: Proceso names the thing first, and abierto follows as its neutral description.
Abierto uses masculine singular -o to match proceso.
En supplies the required relationship, el matches masculine proceso, and que links back to it.
Puede changes for the singular subject cualquiera, while aportar remains in its unchanged -ar dictionary form.
Buenas uses feminine plural -as to match ideas.

regions.labelEs: SÍ, EN OCASIONES HAY TEORÍAS MUY ESTABLECIDAS QUE TERMINAN DERRIBADAS POR SIMPLES EXPERIMENTOS MENTALES.

applications.explanationEn: En ocasiones marks the claim as happening sometimes rather than as a general rule.
Establecidas follows teorías after the intensifier muy as the neutral description.
Establecidas uses feminine plural -as to match teorías.

applications.exampleEs: TEORÍAS MUY ESTABLECIDAS QUE TERMINAN DERRIBADAS
applications.explanationEn: Teorías names what is being described, que links it to the added information, and terminan derribadas supplies that information.
Terminan gives the plural present form, and derribadas describes the feminine plural state reached by the theories.
Both words use their plural forms to name more than one thought experiment.
Experimentos names the tests first, and mentales follows to describe their kind.
Both descriptions use plural forms to match experimentos: simple becomes simples, and mental becomes mentales. Each has the same form with masculine and feminine nouns.

regions.labelEs: Y SÍ, TU LICENCIATURA EN FILOSOFÍA TE CAPACITA PARA PLANTEAR PREGUNTAS INTERESANTES, A VECES.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person being equipped, capacita supplies the present verb, para introduces the enabled action, and plantear stays in its dictionary form.
Preguntas names the things first, and interesantes follows as their neutral description.
Interesantes uses plural -s to match preguntas and keeps the same form for masculine and feminine nouns.
A veces limits the claim to some occasions rather than all the time.

regions.labelEs: PERO NO ACABAS DE DERRIBAR LA RELATIVIDAD ESPECIAL, UN TEMA QUE HAS DESCUBIERTO HACE UNA HORA, CON TU IDEA DEL "COCHE DE CARRERAS SOBRE UN TREN".

applications.explanationEn: Acabas marks one familiar listener and recent time, de links the pattern, and derribar stays in its dictionary form.
Relatividad names the theory first, and especial follows to specify which kind.
Especial stays singular to match relatividad and has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
Tema names what is being described, que links it to the added information, and has descubierto supplies that information.
Has is the form of haber for one familiar listener, and descubierto is the completed-action form of descubrir.
Hace comes before the complete duration una hora to place the discovery that far before the present.
Coche names the car, and de carreras gives its racing purpose.

regions.labelEs: LO QUE PASA ES QUE NO TE GUSTA QUE LE DÉ UN REPASO RACIONAL A TU DOGMA. OYE, ¿CUÁL ES EL EMAIL DEL PRESIDENTE DE LA FÍSICA?

applications.explanationEn: The five-word frame introduces the explanation that follows as the speaker's real point.

applications.exampleEs: NO TE GUSTA QUE LE DÉ
applications.explanationEn: Te gusta expresses the listener's reaction, que introduces what prompts it, and dé uses the special subjunctive form because a separate action is presented through that reaction; no negates the reaction, and le separately points to its target.

applications.exampleEs: LE DÉ UN REPASO RACIONAL A TU DOGMA
applications.explanationEn: Le marks the affected receiver before dé, while a tu dogma explicitly identifies what le refers to.

applications.exampleEs: DÉ UN REPASO RACIONAL A TU DOGMA
applications.explanationEn: Dé un repaso a supplies the review expression, racional separately describes the review, and tu dogma fills the required target slot.
Repaso names the review first, and racional follows as its neutral description.
Racional stays singular to match repaso; this adjective has the same singular form with masculine and feminine nouns.
Oye is the irregular positive command form of oír used to get one familiar listener's attention.
Cuál carries a written accent because it directly asks for the identity of the email address.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the masculine article inside el que (‘which’)
cards.noteEn: After a linking word such as en, el que can refer back to one masculine thing. El matches that earlier thing, while que introduces the added information.

example.es: Ese es el libro en el que aparece la foto.
example.en: That is the book in which the photo appears.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; begins en ocasiones (‘sometimes’)
cards.noteEn: En ocasiones is a fixed time expression meaning that something happens on some occasions rather than always.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something happens sometimes or on some occasions?
cards.noteEn: This fixed expression marks something as occasional rather than constant. Both words stay unchanged, and the expression can appear at the start or later in the statement.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.noteEn: The -as ending matches more than one feminine thing being described.

cards.answerEn: they end up; you all end up (formal)
cards.noteEn: Before a description of the final result, terminan says where people or things eventually end up. It is the present form used with a plural subject.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone or something eventually ends up in a particular state?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of terminar followed by a word that describes the final state.
cards.noteEn: Terminar changes for the person, number, and time. The following description states the result and changes when needed to match what ended up that way: cerrado, cerrada, cerrados, or cerradas.
Derribadas comes from derribar, ‘to knock down’ or ‘overturn.’ Its -adas ending matches more than one feminine thing.

example.en: The barriers were left knocked down.

cards.questionEn: What is the usual Spanish expression for a thought experiment?
cards.answerEn: Use experimento mental; the plural is experimentos mentales.
cards.noteEn: Mental follows experimento and describes an imagined test carried out through reasoning rather than a physical experiment. It changes only for number: mental or mentales.

example.en: They proposed a simple thought experiment.

cards.noteEn: Licenciatura names an undergraduate university qualification. The closest English label varies by education system.

example.en: She has a bachelor's degree in history.

cards.questionEn: Why is the self-proclaimed revolutionary physics argument the joke?
cards.answerEn: The speaker mistakes an hour of reading and one intuitive scenario for a decisive refutation of a deeply tested scientific theory.
cards.noteEn: Special relativity is a foundational, experimentally supported theory rather than a dogma controlled by a single authority. Asking for the ‘president of physics’ extends the joke: science has institutions and experts, but no official who can approve a quick philosophical overthrow of the field.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something equips or qualifies someone to perform an action?
cards.answerEn: Use capacitar a alguien para, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Capacitar changes for the subject and time; the person can also be represented by a short word such as me or te, while para and the following dictionary-form verb keep their roles.

example.es: El curso capacita a Ana para dirigir el equipo.
example.en: The course qualifies Ana to lead the team.

cards.noteEn: Capacita is the present form of capacitar used with one third-person subject. It means giving someone the ability or qualification to do something.

example.es: El curso capacita a los técnicos.

cards.answerEn: to; required after capacitar before the enabled action
cards.noteEn: Capacitar a alguien para hacer algo uses para before the action that the person becomes able or qualified to perform.

example.es: La práctica me capacita para responder.
example.en: The practice equips me to respond.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of a veces, “sometimes”

cards.questionEn: How do you say “sometimes” in Spanish?
cards.noteEn: This common time expression describes something that happens on some occasions but not always. It normally sits before or after the verb without changing form.
In frequency expressions such as a veces and algunas veces, English commonly translates the whole expression as “sometimes.”

cards.answerEn: you have just; you just did (one familiar person)
cards.noteEn: Acabas is a present form of acabar. In acabar de followed by an unchanged action verb, it places that action in the very recent past.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action happened just now?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of acabar, then de, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The final verb stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form. Acabo de means “I have just,” acaba de means “he, she, or formal you has just,” and acabamos de means “we have just.” This pattern talks about recent time; it does not mean literally finishing the later action.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; links acabar to a just-completed action
cards.noteEn: In acabar de plus an unchanged action verb, de is required even though natural English does not translate it separately.
Tema can mean a subject being discussed or studied. This is separate from its use for a musical theme or tune.

example.es: Es un tema difícil de explicar.
example.en: It is a difficult subject to explain.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.answerEn: discovered; found (completed-action form used after haber)
cards.noteEn: Descubierto is the irregular completed-action form of descubrir. After a form of haber, it stays unchanged: he descubierto, han descubierto, and so on.

example.en: They have discovered a new error.

cards.noteEn: Before a length of time, hace tells you how long ago something happened. It does not mean “does” in this use.

cards.questionEn: How do you say how long ago a past event happened?
cards.answerEn: Put hace before the length of time.
cards.noteEn: Spanish places hace before a duration: hace dos semanas means “two weeks ago.” The verb that describes the event itself is normally in a past form.

cards.answerEn: one (feminine singular, before a counted noun)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses un before a masculine noun and una before a feminine noun for both the number one and the indefinite article “a.” Context shows whether an exact count matters.
Hora can name a length of sixty minutes as well as a clock time. A number before it makes the measured duration clear.
Idea ends in -a but is a feminine noun: una idea.
Spanish writes de followed by the masculine singular word el as the single word del.

example.es: El color del coche es rojo.
example.en: The color of the car is red.

cards.questionEn: What is a common Spanish expression for a race car?
cards.noteEn: De carreras describes the car by its racing purpose. Carreras remains plural in the expression even when only one car is mentioned.

example.es: Ese coche de carreras es muy rápido.
example.en: That race car is very fast.

cards.answerEn: often no separate English word; links a noun to another noun that names its type or use
cards.noteEn: Spanish often uses de between two nouns where English uses a noun directly before another noun. For example, una taza de café is ‘a coffee cup,’ and material de oficina is ‘office material.’
Carreras literally means races. After de in coche de carreras, it describes a car designed for racing.

example.es: Vieron un coche de carreras rojo.
example.en: They saw a red race car.

cards.noteEn: Sobre can locate one thing above and supported by another. It has a separate common sense meaning ‘about.’

example.es: Las llaves están sobre la mesa.
example.en: The keys are on the table.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

cards.promptEs: lo que pasa es que + explicación
cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the real issue or explanation with ‘the thing is that…’?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que pasa es que, followed by the explanation.
cards.noteEn: The expression frames what follows as the point the speaker wants to clarify. The words in the frame stay in this order; the explanation after que has its own verb changed for its subject and time.

example.es: Lo que pasa es que hoy no puedo.
example.en: The thing is that I cannot today.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que
no separate English word; part of es que
to you; marks one familiar person as the person who likes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, te identifies the person experiencing the liking. The liked thing controls the verb: te gusta una cosa and te gustan varias cosas.

cards.answerEn: Spanish puts that second verb in a special form called the subjunctive.
cards.noteEn: The first part expresses someone’s feeling or reaction. Que means “that” and introduces what they are reacting to. When the part after que has its own doer, Spanish normally changes its verb to the subjunctive: estás becomes estés in the example. English does not need a separate word for this change.
cards.questionEn: What happens to the second verb after phrases such as “I’m glad that…” or “It bothers me that…”?

example.en: I am glad that you are here.

cards.answerEn: you like; is pleasing to you

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cards.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.

cards.questionEn: Why can Spanish use le or les with a verb and then still name the receiver with a phrase beginning with a?
cards.answerEn: Use le or les with the verb, then use a phrase beginning with the word a to identify the receiver explicitly.
cards.noteEn: Le is for one receiver and les for more than one. It normally appears before a conjugated verb, but it can attach to an unchanged verb form, as in darle. The later a phrase clarifies who or what the short marker refers to; Spanish often keeps both pieces even though natural English states the receiver only once. In the prompt, the slash means that le and les are alternatives, each plus sign means “followed by,” and the dots mean that other words may appear between the verb and the named receiver.

cards.answerEn: give; apply (a special form of dar)
cards.noteEn: Dé is a form of dar, ‘to give.’ It appears when the surrounding words present the giving as wanted, rejected, uncertain, or reacted to rather than simply stating it as a fact; the accent distinguishes it from de, ‘of’ or ‘from.’

example.es: Espero que Ana dé una respuesta.
example.en: I hope Ana gives an answer.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone reviews or goes over something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of dar, then un repaso a, followed by the thing being reviewed.
cards.noteEn: Only dar changes for the person and time. Un repaso names the review, and a introduces its target; a describing word can be placed after repaso without changing the pattern.

example.es: Voy a dar un repaso a mis notas.
example.en: I am going to review my notes.

cards.noteEn: In dar un repaso a algo, repaso means a review or careful examination rather than a physical pass by something.

example.es: Di un repaso a mis notas.

cards.answerEn: to; required before what receives a repaso
cards.noteEn: Dar un repaso a algo uses a before the thing that is reviewed or examined.

example.es: Daremos un repaso a los resultados.

cards.noteEn: Oye is the informal singular command form of oír, “to hear.” In conversation it commonly gets one person's attention, like “hey” or “listen.”

example.en: Hey, I need to talk to you.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.answerEn: what; which one (asking for an identity or value)
cards.noteEn: Before es or son, cuál often asks the listener to identify the answer or value. Natural English frequently uses “what” even though cuál is related to “which.”

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
